Title: How did the Arava become the 'Silicon Valley' of Israeli agriculture?
Chunks: 0,1,2,3,4
By PATRICIA GOLAN MARCH 10, 2023 20:53  
As you drive down the steep, winding road from Arad to the Arava Valley, you might wonder how anyone can survive in this barren environment. Located between the towering Edom Mountains of Jordan and the hills of the Negev, much of the area is still pristine wilderness with a stark natural beauty.
Some 130 kilometers north of Eilat along the Israeli-Jordanian border, this arid desert region is considered the most remote part of the country. Yet, in all seven of the central Arava communities – five moshavim (Idan, Hatzeva, Ein Yahav, Zofar and Paran) and two community settlements (Sapir and Zukim) – there are waiting lists of people who want to move there.
When Samantha Levy first arrived in the Arava in 2009 as a new bride from Colombia, there were almost no houses and no place to live. “If you didn’t fall in love with a farmer, you wouldn’t be able to live here. There was no proper medical center, the conditions were really hard, many people left,” says Levy, today a member of the Resource Development team of the Central Arava Regional Council.
> **“If you didn’t fall in love with a farmer, you wouldn’t be able to live here. There was no proper medical center, the conditions were really hard, many people left.”**  
>   
> Samantha Levy
“There was a very high risk that if we didn’t develop the Arava with infrastructure, places to live, employment, quality of life, education, health, security, we wouldn’t be able to survive. No one would come. To bring people here, you need to provide water, sewage, a place to build a house and, of course, employment.”
THAT WAS then. The transformation in the past 10 years of the central Arava desert communities is nothing less than astonishing. The population has nearly trebled, with 8,000 permanent residents in the south and central Arava, as well as 1,000 foreign agricultural students. The central Arava’s 600 agricultural farms today produce more than 50 percent of Israel’s fresh vegetable exports and a sizable percentage of its cut flower exports. This despite an average yearly rainfall of only two inches.

A youngster bites into a giant cabbage (credit: Yud Tzilumim)
“There’s been so much development, so many projects here,” Levy says, adding that the region now enjoys high-end services, schools bursting at the seams, and a world-class medical center in Sapir, where there’s a new sports center with an Olympic swimming pool. Wait. What? An Olympic pool?

### **Where does the Arava get its water from?**
The Arava is not connected to the national water system. Virtually all the water for the region comes from the aquifer one and a half kilometers beneath the surface, which is extracted via 63 drilling wells. This brackish (saline) groundwater is used for irrigating crops and is funneled to desalination plants for drinking water and domestic use.
The idea for the successful utilization of groundwater in the Arava began in the 1950s. Though agronomists insisted at the time that it was impossible to grow crops in the sandy wasteland, the now legendary hydrologist Prof. Arie Issar argued that the Arava desert sat atop groundwater that could be used for agriculture. It was Issar’s findings which ultimately enabled the development of the Negev and the Arava.
Some of the major inventions, innovations and patents in the sphere of water usage and agriculture come from Israel’s southern Negev region, a living laboratory of arid lands science and technology. (One of Israel’s greatest innovations is the drip irrigation system, invented and developed in the mid-1960s.)
Oren Korin, the CEO of the Arava Water and Drainage Authority, the local water expert and successful date farmer, explains that the non-potable brackish underground water is not suitable for all the crops but that dates, watermelons, grapes and peppers do flourish with it. “Most of the crops last for only one season because of the salt build-up which blocks the flow of water. But if we could irrigate with desalinated water, the crops could last 40 years.”
But the underground aquifer is not an unlimited source. “The water system is delicate, and without recharging, it wouldn’t be sustainable,” adds Korin. The replenishment is done through agricultural drainage and occasional flooding during the winter rains, captured by reservoirs. Each moshav has a wastewater facility and its own desalination plant for drinking water and domestic use. Thus, the ability to fill the swimming pool.

### **Where does the Arava get its water from?**
The engine behind the development of the physical infrastructure, the creation of job opportunities, and the enhancement of the region’s quality of life in the Arava was provided by the Jewish National Fund – USA’s Blueprint Negev campaign launched at the beginning of the 21st century to help “develop the Negev Desert in a sustainable manner to make it home to Israel’s next generation.” The plan to help solve the immediate financial and bureaucratic problems regarding the building process is part of the JNF-USA’s Housing Development Fund plan. While many of the JNF-USA’s ambitious projects in the first decade of the campaign were aimed for the southern city of Beersheba (which is now undergoing exceptional development), the campaign was expanded to include the Arava.
Korin, who was born and raised in the Arava and whose father was one of the pioneer farmers in the region, admits being amazed at the enormous growth of the area and the high demand for housing. “In 2014, I was skeptical that anyone who wasn’t a farmer would come to live in the Arava. The mayor at the time wanted to create 100 lots, and I said, ‘You’re crazy. Who would come to live here?’ He said, ‘You’ll see.’ Now all the lots on our moshav Hatzeva have been sold, and people are building houses. There’s a waiting list for every community planning extensions. This is amazing,” he marvels.
In addition to the farmers and their families, residents include research scientists, teachers and medical staff. But other professionals are moving there as well. “The COVID pandemic changed all the rules,” Korin points out. “It taught us that you can work from home. Lawyers, graphic designers, hi-tech people, etc., can provide services from far away. You don’t have to live in Tel Aviv.”

### **Where does the Arava get its water from?**
GIANT CABBAGES, long shushka peppers, juicy, sweet tomatoes, strawberries to die for – these “niche” crops are all grown in the Arava desert. The biggest crop in the region is peppers – the best you’ll ever taste. But other produce grown there include table grapes, watermelons, dates, asparagus, broccoli, eggplants, zucchini, mangoes, goldenberries, and the weird hybrid called cucamelon. Most are grown between September and May to take advantage of the mild winters, compared to the European climate. (Most Israeli consumers won’t find this heavenly produce in their local markets; most of it goes to Europe, though locally produced dates reach global markets.)
Almost everything can be grown in the region, actually, if adjustments are devised in the way the plant reacts to salinity and climate. That challenge, in large measure, is the job of the R&D (research and development) center located in the Arava: how much shade to provide, what fertilizers can be used to improve yields. The experimental greenhouses research what future crops might be feasible, since competition with Europe, especially Spain, is demanding.
Welcome to “the Silicon Valley” of Israeli agriculture. The JNF’s catchy slogan is “The Arava is where fertile minds meet barren soil.”
In addition to agriculture, the R&D in the Arava focuses on biotechnology, aquaculture and ecology. One of the most revolutionary research projects involves mining the components of desert plants to treat neuro degenerative diseases. Another is developing the extract of the myrrh plant (“mor” of the Bible) as a basis for cosmetic and pharmaceutical products.
Plantation researcher Dafna Harari showing wax flowers for export. (credit: CENTRAL ARAVA REGIONAL COUNCIL)
Most of the researchers are connected to Ben-Gurion University of the Negev and live in the region. “When we set up the labs with JNF-USA, the idea was to generate more job opportunities and bring more families to the region. That was the deal,” says Levy.

Map showing the Lower and Upper Galilee. The narrow "Galilee Panhandle" to the east may be seen geologically and geographically as a separate area (as part of the Jordan Rift Valley), or as part of historical Galilee. The same applies to the western shore of the Sea of Galilee and the Jordan Valley down to [Beit She'an](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beit_She'an "Beit She'an"), as well as the Jezreel Valley in the south and the coastal strip bordering the Galilee to the west.
**Galilee** (;[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-1)Hebrew: הַגָּלִיל, romanized:_hag-Gālīl_; Ancient Greek: _Galilaia_, lit.'Γαλιλαία'; Latin: _Galilaea_;[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-2)Arabic: الجليل, romanized:_al-Jalīl_) is a region located in northern Israel and southern Lebanon consisting of two parts: the Upper Galilee (הגליל העליון, _hag-Galil ha-ʿElyon_; الجليل الأعلى, _al-Jalīl al-Aʿlā_) and the Lower Galilee (הגליל התחתון, _hag-Galil hat-Taḥton_; الجليل الأسفل, _al-Jalīl al-Asfal_). Other sub-regions are the **Western Galilee** and the Galilee Panhandle.
Galilee encompasses the area north of the Mount Carmel–Mount Gilboa ridge and south of the east–west section of the Litani River. It extends from the Israeli coastal plain and the shores of the Mediterranean Sea with Acre in the west, to the Jordan Valley to the east; and from the Litani in the north plus a piece bordering on the Golan Heights to Dan at the base of Mount Hermon in the northeast, to Mount Carmel and Mount Gilboa in the south._[citation needed_]

In some definitions,_[which?_] it may include the plains of the Jezreel Valley north of Jenin and the [Beit She'an Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beit_She'an_Valley "Beit She'an Valley"), the Sea of Galilee, and the Hula Valley._[citation needed_]

## Etymology
The Galilee is first mentioned in Ancient Egyptianinscriptions from the 15th century BC, chronicling the military campaigns led by Tuthmosis III against Canaanite kings in the region.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-Byrce-3) The Egyptian hieroglyphs can either be read as GLL, or the same as in Akkadian: GRR, _garāru_, meaning 'roll'.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-4)
The region's name in Biblical Hebrew: גָּלִיל, romanized:_gālíl_, means 'district' or 'circle'.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-Placenames-5) The form used in the Hebrew Bible's Isaiah 8:23 (Isaiah 9:1 in the Christian Old Testament) is in the construct state, leading to Hebrew: גְּלִיל הַגּוֹיִם, romanized:_gəlil haggóyim_ "Galilee of the nations", which refers to gentiles who settled there at the time the book was written, either by their own volition or as a result of the resettlement policy of the Neo-Assyrian Empire.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-Placenames-5) The region is also referred to as the "land of Naphtali" or "country of Naphtali", in 2 Kings 15:29, after the eponymous tribe of Israel.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-6)

## Etymology
The region's Arabic name is الجليل, _Al-Jalil_, meaning "illustrious" or "grand", and the 1881 Palestine Exploration Fund survey says it is derived from the Hebrew.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-Palmer-7)Ali Fahmi Khashim's 2005 _Akkadian-Arabic: A Comparative Dictionary and Introduction_ gives the root of _al-Jalil_ as Arabic: جلّ, romanized:_jalla_ meaning "great" and cites it as a cognate of the Sumerian word GAL (cuneiform), also meaning "great".[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-Khasheem-8)

## Borders and geography
Galilee district in Mandatory Palestine (1920-1948).
An orchard in Upper Galilee
The extent of Galilee can be defined in two ways: in more stricter, geological terms, which would exclude the low-lying areas on its margins, or in more fluid historical (political) terms, which are based on the territory's affiliation with one state or administrative unit or another. Either way, it is usually split into Upper Galilee and Lower Galilee. The political-administrative borders of 1st-century Galilee were described by Josephus in his _Jewish War_:[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-Zange-9)
> Now Phoenicia and Syria encompass about the Galilees, which are two, and called the Upper Galilee and the Lower. They are bounded toward the sun-setting, with the borders of the territory belonging to Ptolemais, and by Carmel; which mountain had formerly belonged to the Galileans, but now belonged to the Tyrians; to which mountain adjoins [Gaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaba',_Haifa "Jaba', Haifa"), which is called the City of Horsemen, because those horsemen that were dismissed by Herod the king dwelt therein; they are bounded on the south with Samaria and [Scythopolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beit_She'an "Beit She'an"), as far as the river Jordan; on the east with Hippeae and Gadaris, and also with Gaulonitis, and the borders of the kingdom of Agrippa; its northern parts are bounded by Tyre, and the country of the Tyrians. As for that Galilee which is called the Lower, it extends in length from Tiberias to Zabulon, and of the maritime places Ptolemais is its neighbor; its breadth is from the village called Xaloth, which lies in the great plain, as far as Bersabe, from which beginning also is taken the breadth of the Upper Galilee, as far as the village Baca, which divides the land of the Tyrians from it; its length is also from Meloth to Thella, a village near to Jordan.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-10)

## History
### Roman period
#### Early Roman period
In 4 BCE, a rebel named Judah plundered Galilee's largest city, Sepphoris. According to Josephus, the Syrian governor Publius Quinctilius Varus responded by sacking Sepphoris and selling the population into slavery, but the region's archaeology lacks evidence of such destruction.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-Meyers1999-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-Casey2010-25) After the death of Herod the Great that same year, his son Herod Antipas was appointed as tetrarch of Galilee by the Roman emperor Augustus. Galilee remained a Roman client state and Antipas paid tribute to the Roman Empire in exchange for Roman protection.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-Sanders1993-23)
The Romans did not station troops in Galilee, but threatened to retaliate against anyone who attacked it. As long as he continued to pay tribute, Antipas was permitted to govern however he wished[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-Sanders1993-23) and was permitted to mint his own coinage. Antipas was relatively observant of Jewish laws and customs. Although his palace was decorated with animal carvings, which many Jews regarded as a transgression against the law prohibiting idols, his coins bore only agricultural designs, which his subjects deemed acceptable._[citation needed_]

## History
### Roman period
#### Early Roman period
In general, Antipas was a capable ruler. Josephus does not record any instance of his use of force to put down an uprising and he had a long, prosperous reign. However, many Jews probably resented him as not sufficiently devout.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-Sanders1993-23) Antipas rebuilt the city of Sepphoris,[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-Casey2010-25) and in either 18 CE or 19 CE, he founded the new city of Tiberias. These two cities became Galilee's largest cultural centers.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-Sanders1993-23) They were the main centers of Greco-Roman influence, but were still predominantly Jewish. A massive gap existed between the rich and poor,[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-Casey2010-25) but lack of uprisings suggest that taxes were not exorbitantly high and that most Galileans did not feel their livelihoods were being threatened.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-Sanders1993-23)

## History
### Roman period
#### Early Roman period
Late in his reign, Antipas married his half-niece Herodias, who was already married to one of her other uncles. His wife, whom he divorced, fled to her father Aretas, an Arab king, who invaded Galilee and defeated Antipas's troops before withdrawing. Both Josephus and the Gospel of Mark[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-26) record that the itinerant preacher John the Baptist criticized Antipas over his marriage, and Antipas consequently had him imprisoned and then beheaded.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-Sanders1993-23) In around 39 CE, at the urging of Herodias, Antipas went to Rome to request that he be elevated from the status of tetrarch to the status of king. The Romans found him guilty of storing arms, so he was removed from power and exiled, ending his forty-three-year reign. During the Great Revolt (66–73 CE), a Jewish mob destroyed Herod Antipas's palace.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-Sanders1993-23)
Overall, Galilee under Antipas's rule was marked by significant demographic instability. Diseases like malaria were rampant, internal migration between urban and rural areas were frequent and women generally gave birth at young ages while married to older men. Birth control, including infanticide, was not practiced. Many young men, especially marginal villagers, migrated to urban areas to find wives or alternatively, employment. Finding wives was presumed to be competitive since widows often refused to marry past the age of 30 compared to widowers. According to Jonathan L. Reed, this can provide insight on the tropes of New Testament literature, such as miraculous healings and the itinerant lifestyle of Jesus and his disciples.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-27)

## History
### Roman period
#### Early Roman period
In 66 CE, during the Great Jewish Revolt, Josephus was appointed by the Jerusalem provisional government to command Galilee. The region experienced internal conflicts among cities such as Sepphoris and Tiberias, with factions opposing Josephus's authority and warring for control. Sepphoris and other strong cities attempted to remain neutral by maintaining alliances with Rome. Despite opposition, Josephus managed to secure internal peace and fortified nineteen cities in preparation for the Roman invasion; nearly half of them were uncovered by archaeologists. In 67 CE, the Roman army, led by general Vespasian, arrived in Acre. Josephus's account, _The Jewish War_, details the Roman campaign in Galilee, starting with the siege and capture of Gabara, followed by Jotapata (where Josephus was captured), and continuing with Tiberias, Taricheae, Gamala, Tabor, and ending in Gischala. While not all of Galilee was devastated, the conquered cities were razed, and many inhabitants were sold into slavery.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-:0-13)
Jesus and the miraculous catch of fish, in the Sea of Galilee. Many people in Roman-era Galilee were fishermen.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-Casey2010-25)

## History
### Roman period
#### Late Roman period
Judaism reached its political and cultural zenith in the Galilee during the late second and early third century CE. According to rabbinic sources, Judah ha-Nasi's political leadership was at its strongest in relation to the Jewish community in Syria Palaestina, the Diaspora, and the Roman Authorities during this time. Judah's redaction of the Mishnah at this time period represented the peak of intense cultural activity. Archaeological surveys in the Galilee have revealed that the region experienced its height of thriving settlement during this time.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-Leibner2009-17)
According to medieval Hebrew legend, Shimon bar Yochai, one of the most famed of all the tannaim, wrote the _Zohar_ while living in Galilee.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-28)

## History
### Byzantine period
After the completion of the Mishnah, which marked the conclusion of the tannaitic era, came the period of the _amoraim_. The Jerusalem Talmud, the principal work of the amoraim in Palestine, is primarily discussions and interpretations of the Mishnah, and according to academic research, most of it was edited in Tiberias. The vast majority of the _amoraim_ named there, as well as the majority of the settlements or place names referenced, were Galileans.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-Leibner2009-17) By the middle of the fourth century, the Jerusalem Talmud's compilation and editing processes abruptly came to a halt, as Talmudic scholar Yaacov Sussmann put it: "The development of the Jerusalem Talmud seems to have abruptly ceased, as if severed by a sharp and sudden blade".[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-29)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-Leibner2009-17)

## History
### Ottoman period
Safed
The Jewish population of Galilee increased significantly following their expulsion from Spain and welcome from the Ottoman Empire. The community for a time made Safed an international center of cloth weaving and manufacturing, as well as a key site for Jewish learning.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-jafi-37) Today it remains one of Judaism's four holy cities and a center for kabbalah.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-38)
The Galilee, as part of Safed Sanjak, came under the governance of the Druze emir and Ottoman governor [Fakhr al-Din Ma'n](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fakhr_al-Din_Ma'n "Fakhr al-Din Ma'n") and his family starting in 1602. He forged close ties with the Sunni religious establishment in Safed, including its muftiAhmad al-Khalidi, who acclaimed the improvements in the Galilee's conditions under Fakhr al-Din.

## History
### Ottoman period
These were affirmed in an Ottoman _firman_ from 1605, crediting the Druze emir for "guarding the country, keeping the Bedouins in check, ensuring the welfare and tranquility of the population, promoting agriculture, and increasing prosperity".[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAbu-Husayn198583%E2%80%9384-39) For the first time since the fall of the Crusader state, the Franciscans reestablished a permanent Latin Christian presence in Nazareth when Fakhr al-Din granted them permission to reestablish a church at the site of the Annunciation in 1620.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEmmett1995101-40) The [Ma'n dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ma'n_dynasty "Ma'n dynasty") of tax farmers continued to govern the Galilee, with some interruption, until 1660, when the Ottomans administratively reorganized the region.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFirro199245-41) The Druze presence in the Galilee, which dated from the 11th century, was reinforced under the Ma'ns.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFirro199243%E2%80%9345-42) Their rule also saw the establishment or revival of Greek Orthodox Christian communities.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKhamisy20182-43)

## History
### Ottoman period
After 1660, the administration of the Galilee becomes less clear, with the traveler Evliya Celebi noting the _liwa_ s of Safed and Acre. By the end of the 17th century or start of the 18th century, the Galilee, commonly referred to then as _bilad Safad_ (lands of Safed), was administratively divided into lower-tier nahiyes (subdistricts), also called _[mukataa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muqata'ah "Muqata'ah")_ s (fiscal districts), of Sidon Eyalet.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-FOOTNOTECohen1973120%E2%80%93121,_123-44) These were often farmed out by the Ottomans to local _multezim_ s (tax farmers), who were also responsible for protecting and developing their areas, sometimes through the Druze emirs of Mount Lebanon as intermediaries.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-FOOTNOTECohen19737%E2%80%938,_123%E2%80%93124-45) In 1698, Bashir Shihab, emir of the Druze, gained the tax farm of _bilad Safad_, after suppressing local Shia clans in neighboring Jabal Amil (southern Lebanon).[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-FOOTNOTECohen19737%E2%80%938-46)

## History
### Ottoman period
The Shihabs entrusted their Galilee tax farms to the Zayadina (sing. Zaydani), a local family of Bedouin origin based in the Tiberias area. The Zaydani sheikhs were already well established potentates in the Galilee, and by the first decade of the 18th century, their members controlled parts of the eastern Galilee, the area around Nazareth, and the western Lower Galilee. Other potentates included the Husayn sheikhs who dominated the plain of Acre from their fortress at Jiddin and the Nafi sheikhs who dominated the countryside around Safed from their fort at Suhmata.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-FOOTNOTECohen19738%E2%80%939,_83%E2%80%9384-47) During this period, there developed increasing demand from European, mainly French, merchants for the Galilee's cotton. The booming trade spurred increased cultivation in the Galilee's villages and enriched the sheikhs and _multezim_ s, especially the Zayadina, who controlled the villages' output. The Zaydani sheikh Daher al-Umar, in alliance with the unruly Banu Saqr tribe of the Beisan Valley, emerged as the paramount sheikh of his family and took over Tiberias from its government appointee in 1730.

## History
### Ottoman period
Over the next ten years, he gained control of the rest of the Galilee countryside, after subduing other local sheikhs and thwarting assaults by the governors of Sidon and Damascus.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-FOOTNOTECohen197310%E2%80%9312,_14%E2%80%9317-48) To establish law and order, Daher suppressed his erstwhile Bedouin allies, who had often raided villages and threatened the roads.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-FOOTNOTECohen197390%E2%80%9391-49) He and his family built and rebuilt forts across the region, the most important at Tiberias, Deir Hanna, Shefa-Amr, Safed and Saffuriya.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-FOOTNOTECohen197383%E2%80%9385,_123%E2%80%93124-50)

When Samantha Levy first arrived in the Arava in 2009 as a new bride from Colombia, there were almost no houses and no place to live. “If you didn’t fall in love with a farmer, you wouldn’t be able to live here. There was no proper medical center, the conditions were really hard, many people left,” says Levy, today a member of the Resource Development team of the Central Arava Regional Council.
> **“If you didn’t fall in love with a farmer, you wouldn’t be able to live here. There was no proper medical center, the conditions were really hard, many people left.”**  
>   
> Samantha Levy
“There was a very high risk that if we didn’t develop the Arava with infrastructure, places to live, employment, quality of life, education, health, security, we wouldn’t be able to survive. No one would come. To bring people here, you need to provide water, sewage, a place to build a house and, of course, employment.”
THAT WAS then. The transformation in the past 10 years of the central Arava desert communities is nothing less than astonishing. The population has nearly trebled, with 8,000 permanent residents in the south and central Arava, as well as 1,000 foreign agricultural students. The central Arava’s 600 agricultural farms today produce more than 50 percent of Israel’s fresh vegetable exports and a sizable percentage of its cut flower exports. This despite an average yearly rainfall of only two inches.

A youngster bites into a giant cabbage (credit: Yud Tzilumim)
“There’s been so much development, so many projects here,” Levy says, adding that the region now enjoys high-end services, schools bursting at the seams, and a world-class medical center in Sapir, where there’s a new sports center with an Olympic swimming pool. Wait. What? An Olympic pool?

### **Where does the Arava get its water from?**
The Arava is not connected to the national water system. Virtually all the water for the region comes from the aquifer one and a half kilometers beneath the surface, which is extracted via 63 drilling wells. This brackish (saline) groundwater is used for irrigating crops and is funneled to desalination plants for drinking water and domestic use.
The idea for the successful utilization of groundwater in the Arava began in the 1950s. Though agronomists insisted at the time that it was impossible to grow crops in the sandy wasteland, the now legendary hydrologist Prof. Arie Issar argued that the Arava desert sat atop groundwater that could be used for agriculture. It was Issar’s findings which ultimately enabled the development of the Negev and the Arava.
Some of the major inventions, innovations and patents in the sphere of water usage and agriculture come from Israel’s southern Negev region, a living laboratory of arid lands science and technology. (One of Israel’s greatest innovations is the drip irrigation system, invented and developed in the mid-1960s.)
Oren Korin, the CEO of the Arava Water and Drainage Authority, the local water expert and successful date farmer, explains that the non-potable brackish underground water is not suitable for all the crops but that dates, watermelons, grapes and peppers do flourish with it. “Most of the crops last for only one season because of the salt build-up which blocks the flow of water. But if we could irrigate with desalinated water, the crops could last 40 years.”
But the underground aquifer is not an unlimited source. “The water system is delicate, and without recharging, it wouldn’t be sustainable,” adds Korin. The replenishment is done through agricultural drainage and occasional flooding during the winter rains, captured by reservoirs. Each moshav has a wastewater facility and its own desalination plant for drinking water and domestic use. Thus, the ability to fill the swimming pool.
texts.3:
### **Where does the Arava get its water from?**
The engine behind the development of the physical infrastructure, the creation of job opportunities, and the enhancement of the region’s quality of life in the Arava was provided by the Jewish National Fund – USA’s Blueprint Negev campaign launched at the beginning of the 21st century to help “develop the Negev Desert in a sustainable manner to make it home to Israel’s next generation.” The plan to help solve the immediate financial and bureaucratic problems regarding the building process is part of the JNF-USA’s Housing Development Fund plan. While many of the JNF-USA’s ambitious projects in the first decade of the campaign were aimed for the southern city of Beersheba (which is now undergoing exceptional development), the campaign was expanded to include the Arava.
Korin, who was born and raised in the Arava and whose father was one of the pioneer farmers in the region, admits being amazed at the enormous growth of the area and the high demand for housing. “In 2014, I was skeptical that anyone who wasn’t a farmer would come to live in the Arava. The mayor at the time wanted to create 100 lots, and I said, ‘You’re crazy. Who would come to live here?’ He said, ‘You’ll see.’ Now all the lots on our moshav Hatzeva have been sold, and people are building houses. There’s a waiting list for every community planning extensions. This is amazing,” he marvels.
In addition to the farmers and their families, residents include research scientists, teachers and medical staff. But other professionals are moving there as well. “The COVID pandemic changed all the rules,” Korin points out. “It taught us that you can work from home. Lawyers, graphic designers, hi-tech people, etc., can provide services from far away. You don’t have to live in Tel Aviv.”
texts.4:
### **Where does the Arava get its water from?**
GIANT CABBAGES, long shushka peppers, juicy, sweet tomatoes, strawberries to die for – these “niche” crops are all grown in the Arava desert. The biggest crop in the region is peppers – the best you’ll ever taste. But other produce grown there include table grapes, watermelons, dates, asparagus, broccoli, eggplants, zucchini, mangoes, goldenberries, and the weird hybrid called cucamelon. Most are grown between September and May to take advantage of the mild winters, compared to the European climate. (Most Israeli consumers won’t find this heavenly produce in their local markets; most of it goes to Europe, though locally produced dates reach global markets.)
Almost everything can be grown in the region, actually, if adjustments are devised in the way the plant reacts to salinity and climate. That challenge, in large measure, is the job of the R&D (research and development) center located in the Arava: how much shade to provide, what fertilizers can be used to improve yields. The experimental greenhouses research what future crops might be feasible, since competition with Europe, especially Spain, is demanding.
Welcome to “the Silicon Valley” of Israeli agriculture. The JNF’s catchy slogan is “The Arava is where fertile minds meet barren soil.”
In addition to agriculture, the R&D in the Arava focuses on biotechnology, aquaculture and ecology. One of the most revolutionary research projects involves mining the components of desert plants to treat neuro degenerative diseases. Another is developing the extract of the myrrh plant (“mor” of the Bible) as a basis for cosmetic and pharmaceutical products.
Plantation researcher Dafna Harari showing wax flowers for export. (credit: CENTRAL ARAVA REGIONAL COUNCIL)
Most of the researchers are connected to Ben-Gurion University of the Negev and live in the region. “When we set up the labs with JNF-USA, the idea was to generate more job opportunities and bring more families to the region. That was the deal,” says Levy.

The narrow "Galilee Panhandle" to the east may be seen geologically and geographically as a separate area (as part of the Jordan Rift Valley), or as part of historical Galilee. The same applies to the western shore of the Sea of Galilee and the Jordan Valley down to [Beit She'an](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beit_She'an "Beit She'an"), as well as the Jezreel Valley in the south and the coastal strip bordering the Galilee to the west.
**Galilee** (;[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-1)Hebrew: הַגָּלִיל, romanized:_hag-Gālīl_; Ancient Greek: _Galilaia_, lit.'Γαλιλαία'; Latin: _Galilaea_;[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-2)Arabic: الجليل, romanized:_al-Jalīl_) is a region located in northern Israel and southern Lebanon consisting of two parts: the Upper Galilee (הגליל העליון, _hag-Galil ha-ʿElyon_; الجليل الأعلى, _al-Jalīl al-Aʿlā_) and the Lower Galilee (הגליל התחתון, _hag-Galil hat-Taḥton_; الجليل الأسفل, _al-Jalīl al-Asfal_). Other sub-regions are the **Western Galilee** and the Galilee Panhandle.
Galilee encompasses the area north of the Mount Carmel–Mount Gilboa ridge and south of the east–west section of the Litani River. It extends from the Israeli coastal plain and the shores of the Mediterranean Sea with Acre in the west, to the Jordan Valley to the east; and from the Litani in the north plus a piece bordering on the Golan Heights to Dan at the base of Mount Hermon in the northeast, to Mount Carmel and Mount Gilboa in the south._[citation needed_]
texts.1: In some definitions,_[which?_] it may include the plains of the Jezreel Valley north of Jenin and the [Beit She'an Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beit_She'an_Valley "Beit She'an Valley"), the Sea of Galilee, and the Hula Valley._[citation needed_]

## Etymology
The Galilee is first mentioned in Ancient Egyptianinscriptions from the 15th century BC, chronicling the military campaigns led by Tuthmosis III against Canaanite kings in the region.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-Byrce-3) The Egyptian hieroglyphs can either be read as GLL, or the same as in Akkadian: GRR, _garāru_, meaning 'roll'.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-4)
The region's name in Biblical Hebrew: גָּלִיל, romanized:_gālíl_, means 'district' or 'circle'.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-Placenames-5) The form used in the Hebrew Bible's Isaiah 8:23 (Isaiah 9:1 in the Christian Old Testament) is in the construct state, leading to Hebrew: גְּלִיל הַגּוֹיִם, romanized:_gəlil haggóyim_ "Galilee of the nations", which refers to gentiles who settled there at the time the book was written, either by their own volition or as a result of the resettlement policy of the Neo-Assyrian Empire.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-Placenames-5) The region is also referred to as the "land of Naphtali" or "country of Naphtali", in 2 Kings 15:29, after the eponymous tribe of Israel.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-6)

## Etymology
The region's Arabic name is الجليل, _Al-Jalil_, meaning "illustrious" or "grand", and the 1881 Palestine Exploration Fund survey says it is derived from the Hebrew.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-Palmer-7)Ali Fahmi Khashim's 2005 _Akkadian-Arabic: A Comparative Dictionary and Introduction_ gives the root of _al-Jalil_ as Arabic: جلّ, romanized:_jalla_ meaning "great" and cites it as a cognate of the Sumerian word GAL (cuneiform), also meaning "great".[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-Khasheem-8)

## Borders and geography
Galilee district in Mandatory Palestine (1920-1948).
An orchard in Upper Galilee
The extent of Galilee can be defined in two ways: in more stricter, geological terms, which would exclude the low-lying areas on its margins, or in more fluid historical (political) terms, which are based on the territory's affiliation with one state or administrative unit or another. Either way, it is usually split into Upper Galilee and Lower Galilee. The political-administrative borders of 1st-century Galilee were described by Josephus in his _Jewish War_:[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-Zange-9)
> Now Phoenicia and Syria encompass about the Galilees, which are two, and called the Upper Galilee and the Lower. They are bounded toward the sun-setting, with the borders of the territory belonging to Ptolemais, and by Carmel; which mountain had formerly belonged to the Galileans, but now belonged to the Tyrians; to which mountain adjoins [Gaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaba',_Haifa "Jaba', Haifa"), which is called the City of Horsemen, because those horsemen that were dismissed by Herod the king dwelt therein; they are bounded on the south with Samaria and [Scythopolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beit_She'an "Beit She'an"), as far as the river Jordan; on the east with Hippeae and Gadaris, and also with Gaulonitis, and the borders of the kingdom of Agrippa; its northern parts are bounded by Tyre, and the country of the Tyrians. As for that Galilee which is called the Lower, it extends in length from Tiberias to Zabulon, and of the maritime places Ptolemais is its neighbor; its breadth is from the village called Xaloth, which lies in the great plain, as far as Bersabe, from which beginning also is taken the breadth of the Upper Galilee, as far as the village Baca, which divides the land of the Tyrians from it; its length is also from Meloth to Thella, a village near to Jordan.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-10)

## History
### Roman period
#### Early Roman period
In 4 BCE, a rebel named Judah plundered Galilee's largest city, Sepphoris. According to Josephus, the Syrian governor Publius Quinctilius Varus responded by sacking Sepphoris and selling the population into slavery, but the region's archaeology lacks evidence of such destruction.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-Meyers1999-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-Casey2010-25) After the death of Herod the Great that same year, his son Herod Antipas was appointed as tetrarch of Galilee by the Roman emperor Augustus. Galilee remained a Roman client state and Antipas paid tribute to the Roman Empire in exchange for Roman protection.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-Sanders1993-23)
The Romans did not station troops in Galilee, but threatened to retaliate against anyone who attacked it. As long as he continued to pay tribute, Antipas was permitted to govern however he wished[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-Sanders1993-23) and was permitted to mint his own coinage. Antipas was relatively observant of Jewish laws and customs. Although his palace was decorated with animal carvings, which many Jews regarded as a transgression against the law prohibiting idols, his coins bore only agricultural designs, which his subjects deemed acceptable._[citation needed_]
texts.13:
## History
### Roman period
#### Early Roman period
In general, Antipas was a capable ruler. Josephus does not record any instance of his use of force to put down an uprising and he had a long, prosperous reign. However, many Jews probably resented him as not sufficiently devout.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-Sanders1993-23) Antipas rebuilt the city of Sepphoris,[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-Casey2010-25) and in either 18 CE or 19 CE, he founded the new city of Tiberias. These two cities became Galilee's largest cultural centers.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-Sanders1993-23) They were the main centers of Greco-Roman influence, but were still predominantly Jewish. A massive gap existed between the rich and poor,[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-Casey2010-25) but lack of uprisings suggest that taxes were not exorbitantly high and that most Galileans did not feel their livelihoods were being threatened.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-Sanders1993-23)
texts.14:
## History
### Roman period
#### Early Roman period
Late in his reign, Antipas married his half-niece Herodias, who was already married to one of her other uncles. His wife, whom he divorced, fled to her father Aretas, an Arab king, who invaded Galilee and defeated Antipas's troops before withdrawing. Both Josephus and the Gospel of Mark[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-26) record that the itinerant preacher John the Baptist criticized Antipas over his marriage, and Antipas consequently had him imprisoned and then beheaded.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-Sanders1993-23) In around 39 CE, at the urging of Herodias, Antipas went to Rome to request that he be elevated from the status of tetrarch to the status of king. The Romans found him guilty of storing arms, so he was removed from power and exiled, ending his forty-three-year reign. During the Great Revolt (66–73 CE), a Jewish mob destroyed Herod Antipas's palace.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-Sanders1993-23)
Overall, Galilee under Antipas's rule was marked by significant demographic instability. Diseases like malaria were rampant, internal migration between urban and rural areas were frequent and women generally gave birth at young ages while married to older men. Birth control, including infanticide, was not practiced. Many young men, especially marginal villagers, migrated to urban areas to find wives or alternatively, employment. Finding wives was presumed to be competitive since widows often refused to marry past the age of 30 compared to widowers. According to Jonathan L. Reed, this can provide insight on the tropes of New Testament literature, such as miraculous healings and the itinerant lifestyle of Jesus and his disciples.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-27)

## History
### Roman period
#### Early Roman period
In 66 CE, during the Great Jewish Revolt, Josephus was appointed by the Jerusalem provisional government to command Galilee. The region experienced internal conflicts among cities such as Sepphoris and Tiberias, with factions opposing Josephus's authority and warring for control. Sepphoris and other strong cities attempted to remain neutral by maintaining alliances with Rome. Despite opposition, Josephus managed to secure internal peace and fortified nineteen cities in preparation for the Roman invasion; nearly half of them were uncovered by archaeologists. In 67 CE, the Roman army, led by general Vespasian, arrived in Acre. Josephus's account, _The Jewish War_, details the Roman campaign in Galilee, starting with the siege and capture of Gabara, followed by Jotapata (where Josephus was captured), and continuing with Tiberias, Taricheae, Gamala, Tabor, and ending in Gischala. While not all of Galilee was devastated, the conquered cities were razed, and many inhabitants were sold into slavery.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-:0-13)
Jesus and the miraculous catch of fish, in the Sea of Galilee. Many people in Roman-era Galilee were fishermen.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-Casey2010-25)

## History
### Roman period
#### Late Roman period
Judaism reached its political and cultural zenith in the Galilee during the late second and early third century CE. According to rabbinic sources, Judah ha-Nasi's political leadership was at its strongest in relation to the Jewish community in Syria Palaestina, the Diaspora, and the Roman Authorities during this time. Judah's redaction of the Mishnah at this time period represented the peak of intense cultural activity. Archaeological surveys in the Galilee have revealed that the region experienced its height of thriving settlement during this time.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-Leibner2009-17)
According to medieval Hebrew legend, Shimon bar Yochai, one of the most famed of all the tannaim, wrote the _Zohar_ while living in Galilee.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-28)
texts.17:
## History
### Byzantine period
After the completion of the Mishnah, which marked the conclusion of the tannaitic era, came the period of the _amoraim_. The Jerusalem Talmud, the principal work of the amoraim in Palestine, is primarily discussions and interpretations of the Mishnah, and according to academic research, most of it was edited in Tiberias. The vast majority of the _amoraim_ named there, as well as the majority of the settlements or place names referenced, were Galileans.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-Leibner2009-17) By the middle of the fourth century, the Jerusalem Talmud's compilation and editing processes abruptly came to a halt, as Talmudic scholar Yaacov Sussmann put it: "The development of the Jerusalem Talmud seems to have abruptly ceased, as if severed by a sharp and sudden blade".[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-29)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-Leibner2009-17)

## History
### Ottoman period
Safed
The Jewish population of Galilee increased significantly following their expulsion from Spain and welcome from the Ottoman Empire. The community for a time made Safed an international center of cloth weaving and manufacturing, as well as a key site for Jewish learning.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-jafi-37) Today it remains one of Judaism's four holy cities and a center for kabbalah.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-38)
The Galilee, as part of Safed Sanjak, came under the governance of the Druze emir and Ottoman governor [Fakhr al-Din Ma'n](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fakhr_al-Din_Ma'n "Fakhr al-Din Ma'n") and his family starting in 1602. He forged close ties with the Sunni religious establishment in Safed, including its muftiAhmad al-Khalidi, who acclaimed the improvements in the Galilee's conditions under Fakhr al-Din.

## History
### Ottoman period
These were affirmed in an Ottoman _firman_ from 1605, crediting the Druze emir for "guarding the country, keeping the Bedouins in check, ensuring the welfare and tranquility of the population, promoting agriculture, and increasing prosperity".[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-FOOTNOTEAbu-Husayn198583%E2%80%9384-39) For the first time since the fall of the Crusader state, the Franciscans reestablished a permanent Latin Christian presence in Nazareth when Fakhr al-Din granted them permission to reestablish a church at the site of the Annunciation in 1620.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-FOOTNOTEEmmett1995101-40) The [Ma'n dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ma'n_dynasty "Ma'n dynasty") of tax farmers continued to govern the Galilee, with some interruption, until 1660, when the Ottomans administratively reorganized the region.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFirro199245-41) The Druze presence in the Galilee, which dated from the 11th century, was reinforced under the Ma'ns.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFirro199243%E2%80%9345-42) Their rule also saw the establishment or revival of Greek Orthodox Christian communities.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKhamisy20182-43)

## History
### Ottoman period
After 1660, the administration of the Galilee becomes less clear, with the traveler Evliya Celebi noting the _liwa_ s of Safed and Acre. By the end of the 17th century or start of the 18th century, the Galilee, commonly referred to then as _bilad Safad_ (lands of Safed), was administratively divided into lower-tier nahiyes (subdistricts), also called _[mukataa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muqata'ah "Muqata'ah")_ s (fiscal districts), of Sidon Eyalet.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-FOOTNOTECohen1973120%E2%80%93121,_123-44) These were often farmed out by the Ottomans to local _multezim_ s (tax farmers), who were also responsible for protecting and developing their areas, sometimes through the Druze emirs of Mount Lebanon as intermediaries.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-FOOTNOTECohen19737%E2%80%938,_123%E2%80%93124-45) In 1698, Bashir Shihab, emir of the Druze, gained the tax farm of _bilad Safad_, after suppressing local Shia clans in neighboring Jabal Amil (southern Lebanon).[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-FOOTNOTECohen19737%E2%80%938-46)
texts.25:
## History
### Ottoman period
The Shihabs entrusted their Galilee tax farms to the Zayadina (sing. Zaydani), a local family of Bedouin origin based in the Tiberias area. The Zaydani sheikhs were already well established potentates in the Galilee, and by the first decade of the 18th century, their members controlled parts of the eastern Galilee, the area around Nazareth, and the western Lower Galilee. Other potentates included the Husayn sheikhs who dominated the plain of Acre from their fortress at Jiddin and the Nafi sheikhs who dominated the countryside around Safed from their fort at Suhmata.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-FOOTNOTECohen19738%E2%80%939,_83%E2%80%9384-47) During this period, there developed increasing demand from European, mainly French, merchants for the Galilee's cotton. The booming trade spurred increased cultivation in the Galilee's villages and enriched the sheikhs and _multezim_ s, especially the Zayadina, who controlled the villages' output. The Zaydani sheikh Daher al-Umar, in alliance with the unruly Banu Saqr tribe of the Beisan Valley, emerged as the paramount sheikh of his family and took over Tiberias from its government appointee in 1730.
texts.26:
## History
### Ottoman period
Over the next ten years, he gained control of the rest of the Galilee countryside, after subduing other local sheikhs and thwarting assaults by the governors of Sidon and Damascus.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-FOOTNOTECohen197310%E2%80%9312,_14%E2%80%9317-48) To establish law and order, Daher suppressed his erstwhile Bedouin allies, who had often raided villages and threatened the roads.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-FOOTNOTECohen197390%E2%80%9391-49) He and his family built and rebuilt forts across the region, the most important at Tiberias, Deir Hanna, Shefa-Amr, Safed and Saffuriya.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galilee#cite_note-FOOTNOTECohen197383%E2%80%9385,_123%E2%80%93124-50)

The **Navigation Acts**, or more broadly the **Acts of Trade and Navigation**, were a series of English laws that developed, promoted, and regulated English ships, shipping, trade, and commerce with other countries and with its own colonies. The laws also regulated England's fisheries and restricted foreign—including Scottish and Irish—participation in its colonial trade.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navigation_Acts#cite_note-1) The first such laws enacted in 1650 and 1651 under the Commonwealth of England under Oliver Cromwell.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navigation_Acts#cite_note-2)
With the Restoration in 1660, royal government passed the Navigation Act 1660,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navigation_Acts#cite_note-3) and then further developed and tightened by the Navigation Acts of 1663, 1673, and 1696.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navigation_Acts#cite_note-Purvis1997-4) Upon this basis during the 18th century, the acts were modified by subsequent amendments, changes, and the addition of enforcement mechanisms and staff. A major change in the purpose of the acts began in the 1760s, with the aim of generating revenue, i.e., taxes, from the colonies, rather than solely regulating trade. Colonists in North America saw the change in royal policy as trampling their rights as Englishmen and resisted what they considered taxation without representation,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navigation_Acts#cite_note-5) and significant changes in the implementation of the acts themselves.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navigation_Acts#cite_note-6)

The acts generally prohibited the use of foreign ships, required the employment of English and colonial mariners for 75% of the crews, including East India Company ships. The acts prohibited colonies from exporting certain products to countries other than Britain and those countries' colonies, and mandated that imports be sourced only through Britain.
Overall, the acts formed the basis for English (and later) British overseas trade for nearly 200 years, but with the development and gradual acceptance of free trade, the acts were eventually repealed in 1849. The laws reflected the European economic theory of mercantilism which sought to keep all the benefits of trade inside their respective empires, and to minimize the loss of gold and silver, or profits, to foreigners through purchases and trade. The system would develop with the colonies supplying raw materials for British industry, and in exchange for this guaranteed market, the colonies would purchase manufactured goods from or through Britain.
The major impetus for the first Navigation Act was the ruinous deterioration of English trade in the [aftermath of the Eighty Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aftermath_of_the_Eighty_Years'_War "Aftermath of the Eighty Years' War"), and the associated lifting of the Spanish embargoes on trade between the Spanish Empire and the Dutch Republic. The end of the embargoes in 1647 unleashed the full power of the Amsterdam Entrepôt and other Dutch competitive advantages in European and world trade. Within a few years, English merchants had practically been overwhelmed in the Baltic and North Sea trade, as well as trade with the Iberian Peninsula, the Mediterranean and the Levant. Even the trade with English colonies (partly still in the hands of the royalists, as the English Civil War was in its final stages and the Commonwealth of England had not yet imposed its authority throughout the English colonies - see English overseas possessions in the Wars of the Three Kingdoms) was "engrossed" by Dutch merchants. English direct trade was crowded out by a sudden influx of commodities from the Levant, Mediterranean and the Spanish and Portuguese empires, and the West Indies via the Dutch entrepôt, carried in Dutch ships and for Dutch account.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navigation_Acts#cite_note-7)

The obvious solution seemed to be to seal off the English markets to these unwanted imports. A precedent was the act the Greenland Company had obtained from Parliament in 1645 prohibiting the import of whale products into England, except in ships owned by that company. This principle was now generalized. In 1648 the Levant Company petitioned Parliament for the prohibition of imports of Turkish goods "...from Holland and other places but directly from the places of their growth."[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navigation_Acts#cite_note-8) Baltic traders added their voices to this chorus. In 1650 the Standing Council for Trade and the Council of State of the Commonwealth prepared a general policy designed to impede the flow of Mediterranean and colonial commodities via Holland and Zeeland into England.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navigation_Acts#cite_note-9)
Following the 1696 act, the acts of Trade and Navigation were generally obeyed, except for the Molasses Act 1733, which led to extensive smuggling because no effective means of enforcement was provided until the 1760s. Stricter enforcement under the Sugar Act 1764 became one source of resentment among merchants in the American colonies towards Great Britain. This, in turn, helped push the American colonies to rebel in the late 18th century, even though the consensus view among modern economic historians and economists is that the "costs imposed on [American] colonists by the trade restrictions of the Navigation Acts were small."[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navigation_Acts#cite_note-Whaples_March_1995_140-10)

## Historical precedents
[edit]
Some principles of English mercantile legislation pre-date both the passage of the Navigation Act 1651 and the settlement of England's early foreign possessions. A 1381 Act[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navigation_Acts#cite_note-11) passed under King Richard II provided "that, to increase the navy of England, no goods or merchandises shall be either exported or imported, but only in ships belonging to the King's subjects." The letters patent granted to the Cabots by Henry VII in 1498 stipulated that the commerce resulting from their discoveries must be with England (specifically Bristol).[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navigation_Acts#cite_note-12) Henry VIII established a second principle by statute: that such a vessel must be English-built and a majority of the crew must be English-born. Legislation during the reign of Elizabeth I also dealt with these questions and resulted in a large increase in English merchant shipping.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navigation_Acts#cite_note-ColSelf1-13) Soon after actual settlements had been made in America, these early requirements illustrate the English theory then held regarding the governmental control of maritime commerce.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navigation_Acts#cite_note-ComPolE-14)
With the establishment of overseas colonies a distinct colonial policy began to develop, and the principles embodied in the early Navigation and Trade Acts also had some more immediate precedents in the provisions of the charters granted to the London and Plymouth Company, in the various royal patents later bestowed by Charles I and Charles II, as well as in the early regulations concerning the tobacco trade, the first profitable colonial export. An Order in Council of 24 October 1621 prohibited the Colony of Virginia to export tobacco and other commodities to foreign countries.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navigation_Acts#cite_note-AndrCofT&P-15)

# Plan Your Time in Bruges
## Tallinn, Estonia: A Well-Preserved City of the Hanseatic League
Tallinn, Estonia, exceptionally well-preserved as a complete medieval city, served as a significant Hanseatic League outpost controlling trade with Russia after Novgorod’s accessibility declined. The entire old town is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, with intact city walls, towers, and a street pattern little changed since the Hanseatic era.
The Great Guild Hall, built in the 1410s, housed Tallinn’s most important merchant association and now contains part of the Estonian History Museum with exhibits on Hanseatic trade. Address: Pikk 17, 10133 Tallinn, Estonia. Website: www.ajaloomuuseum.ee.
St. Olaf’s Church, whose spire once made it one of the tallest buildings in the world, symbolized Tallinn’s (then known as Reval) wealth and importance to the Hanseatic League. Address: Lai 50, 10133 Tallinn, Estonia. Website: www.oleviste.ee.
The medieval Town Hall Square, surrounded by merchant houses with stepped gables, presents an ensemble of Hanseatic architecture little changed in its essential character. Address: Raekoja plats 1, 10146 Tallinn, Estonia.

# Plan Your Time in Bruges
## Visby, Sweden: A UNESCO City of the Hanseatic League
Visby, located on the Swedish island of Gotland in the Baltic Sea, was an early leader in Baltic trade before being eclipsed by mainland cities and suffering conquest by Denmark in 1361. The city’s medieval walls survive almost completely intact, encircling a town center where ruined churches and preserved merchant houses testify to Visby’s Hanseatic past.
The Gotland Museum presents exhibits on the island’s medieval prosperity and its role in the Hanseatic League, including hoards of coins that reveal the extent of Visby’s trading connections. Address: Strandgatan 14, 621 56. Website: www.gotlandsmuseum.se.
The entire medieval town of Visby is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and walking its streets provides a sense of a Hanseatic city frozen at an earlier moment in the confederation’s development, before the later elaboration seen in cities that remained prosperous longer.
These cities represent only the most accessible and well-preserved examples of Hanseatic heritage available to travelers in 2026. Many other former members of the Hanseatic League—Riga, Rostock, Stralsund, Wismar, Kampen, Deventer—also preserve significant medieval architecture and maintain museums exploring their Hanseatic past. For cruise passengers with limited time in port, prioritizing the old town centers of these cities and seeking out the characteristic elements of Hanseatic architecture—brick Gothic churches, stepped-gable merchant houses, medieval warehouses, and harbor installations—will provide the most rewarding encounters with this remarkable historical confederation. The legacy of the Hanseatic League offers a lens through which to understand northern Europe’s medieval development and to appreciate how commercial enterprise and urban culture created a prosperous, interconnected world centuries before our modern age of globalization.

## **The Decline and Dissolution of the Hanseatic League**


# Plan Your Time in Bruges
## **The Hanseatic League’s Enduring Significance**
Changing patterns of global trade gradually undermined the Hanseatic League’s commercial position. The confederation had thrived by controlling trade routes in the Baltic and North Seasand by connecting northern Europe’s regional markets. The discovery of the Americas and the opening of oceanic trade routes to Asia shifted Europe’s commercial center of gravity southward and westward, toward the Atlantic ports of Portugal, Spain, the Netherlands, and England.
While some Hanseatic cities, particularly Hamburg, adapted by engaging with Atlantic trade, the Hanseatic League as a confederation lacked the flexibility to reorient its collective strategy. The commodities that had formed the basis of Hanseatic prosperity—Baltic grain, timber, furs, and stockfish—remained important but declined in relative value compared to colonial products like sugar, tobacco, and eventually silver from American mines. The Hanseatic League found itself marginalized in the new global commercial order, its carefully cultivated privileges and trade routes bypassed by merchants operating on oceanic scales and bringing exotic goods that commanded premium prices.
New forms of commercial organization and financial practice challenged the Hanseatic League’s traditional methods. Joint-stock companies, pioneered by Dutch and English merchants, could raise larger amounts of capital and spread risk across more investors than the Hanseatic League’s family-based merchant houses. Sophisticated financial instruments developed in Amsterdam and London—futures contracts, marine insurance, negotiable bills of exchange—facilitated commerce in ways that made the Hanseatic League’s practices seem antiquated.
Banking and credit systems too became more complex and more centralized, creating dependencies that worked against the Hanseatic League’s model of distributed commercial activity. The confederation’s conservative merchant oligarchs, whose wealth was tied up in traditional trades and established privileges, often resisted innovation, preferring to defend what they had rather than risk change. This conservatism, while understandable, left the Hanseatic League increasingly unable to compete with more nimble and innovative competitors.

# Plan Your Time in Bruges
## **The Hanseatic League’s Enduring Significance**
Religious conflict and war devastated many Hanseatic League cities during the Reformation and the Thirty Years’ War (1618-1648). The Protestant Reformation split the Hanseatic League along religious lines, with some cities adopting Lutheranism while others remained Catholic or embraced other Protestant variants. These religious divisions complicated the confederation’s governance and made unified action more difficult. More catastrophically, the Thirty Years’ War turned much of northern Germany into a battlefield, disrupting trade routes, destroying property, and killing or displacing large portions of the population.
Hanseatic League member cities found themselves unable to remain neutral in this conflict, as competing armies demanded support and punished those who provided aid to enemies. The economic devastation of this prolonged war weakened even those Hanseatic cities that had not been directly besieged or occupied, as trade networks collapsed and commercial confidence evaporated. The Hanseatic League never recovered from this catastrophe, though the confederation officially lingered until 1669, when its last Hansetag convened in Lübeck with representatives from only nine cities.
By the late seventeenth century, the Hanseatic League had effectively ceased to function as a meaningful organization, though individual former member cities—Hamburg, Lübeck, Bremen—retained their wealth and importance as trading centers. The confederation’s physical Kontore had been closed or lost their privileges: the London Steelyard shut down in 1598, the Novgorod Peterhof had ended in the 1490s, the Bergen operation gradually came under Norwegian and Danish control. Some Hanseatic privileges survived in vestigial form, but the coordinated network that had once dominated northern European commerce had dissolved. The three cities of Hamburg, Lübeck, and Bremen retained the title “Hanseatic City” (Hansestadt) as a mark of pride and historical continuity—a title they still use today—but the Hanseatic League as a living institution had passed into history. Its decline illustrated how even powerful and successful organizations cannot adapt when fundamental conditions change, and how privileges and practices that once conferred advantage can become obstacles when circumstances demand flexibility and innovation.

The **Navigation Acts**, or more broadly the **Acts of Trade and Navigation**, were a series of English laws that developed, promoted, and regulated English ships, shipping, trade, and commerce with other countries and with its own colonies. The laws also regulated England's fisheries and restricted foreign—including Scottish and Irish—participation in its colonial trade.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navigation_Acts#cite_note-1) The first such laws enacted in 1650 and 1651 under the Commonwealth of England under Oliver Cromwell.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navigation_Acts#cite_note-2)
With the Restoration in 1660, royal government passed the Navigation Act 1660,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navigation_Acts#cite_note-3) and then further developed and tightened by the Navigation Acts of 1663, 1673, and 1696.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navigation_Acts#cite_note-Purvis1997-4) Upon this basis during the 18th century, the acts were modified by subsequent amendments, changes, and the addition of enforcement mechanisms and staff. A major change in the purpose of the acts began in the 1760s, with the aim of generating revenue, i.e., taxes, from the colonies, rather than solely regulating trade. Colonists in North America saw the change in royal policy as trampling their rights as Englishmen and resisted what they considered taxation without representation,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navigation_Acts#cite_note-5) and significant changes in the implementation of the acts themselves.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navigation_Acts#cite_note-6)
texts.1:
The acts generally prohibited the use of foreign ships, required the employment of English and colonial mariners for 75% of the crews, including East India Company ships. The acts prohibited colonies from exporting certain products to countries other than Britain and those countries' colonies, and mandated that imports be sourced only through Britain.
Overall, the acts formed the basis for English (and later) British overseas trade for nearly 200 years, but with the development and gradual acceptance of free trade, the acts were eventually repealed in 1849. The laws reflected the European economic theory of mercantilism which sought to keep all the benefits of trade inside their respective empires, and to minimize the loss of gold and silver, or profits, to foreigners through purchases and trade. The system would develop with the colonies supplying raw materials for British industry, and in exchange for this guaranteed market, the colonies would purchase manufactured goods from or through Britain.
The major impetus for the first Navigation Act was the ruinous deterioration of English trade in the [aftermath of the Eighty Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aftermath_of_the_Eighty_Years'_War "Aftermath of the Eighty Years' War"), and the associated lifting of the Spanish embargoes on trade between the Spanish Empire and the Dutch Republic. The end of the embargoes in 1647 unleashed the full power of the Amsterdam Entrepôt and other Dutch competitive advantages in European and world trade. Within a few years, English merchants had practically been overwhelmed in the Baltic and North Sea trade, as well as trade with the Iberian Peninsula, the Mediterranean and the Levant. Even the trade with English colonies (partly still in the hands of the royalists, as the English Civil War was in its final stages and the Commonwealth of England had not yet imposed its authority throughout the English colonies - see English overseas possessions in the Wars of the Three Kingdoms) was "engrossed" by Dutch merchants. English direct trade was crowded out by a sudden influx of commodities from the Levant, Mediterranean and the Spanish and Portuguese empires, and the West Indies via the Dutch entrepôt, carried in Dutch ships and for Dutch account.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navigation_Acts#cite_note-7)

The obvious solution seemed to be to seal off the English markets to these unwanted imports. A precedent was the act the Greenland Company had obtained from Parliament in 1645 prohibiting the import of whale products into England, except in ships owned by that company. This principle was now generalized. In 1648 the Levant Company petitioned Parliament for the prohibition of imports of Turkish goods "...from Holland and other places but directly from the places of their growth."[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navigation_Acts#cite_note-8) Baltic traders added their voices to this chorus. In 1650 the Standing Council for Trade and the Council of State of the Commonwealth prepared a general policy designed to impede the flow of Mediterranean and colonial commodities via Holland and Zeeland into England.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navigation_Acts#cite_note-9)
Following the 1696 act, the acts of Trade and Navigation were generally obeyed, except for the Molasses Act 1733, which led to extensive smuggling because no effective means of enforcement was provided until the 1760s. Stricter enforcement under the Sugar Act 1764 became one source of resentment among merchants in the American colonies towards Great Britain. This, in turn, helped push the American colonies to rebel in the late 18th century, even though the consensus view among modern economic historians and economists is that the "costs imposed on [American] colonists by the trade restrictions of the Navigation Acts were small."[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navigation_Acts#cite_note-Whaples_March_1995_140-10)

## Historical precedents
[edit]
Some principles of English mercantile legislation pre-date both the passage of the Navigation Act 1651 and the settlement of England's early foreign possessions. A 1381 Act[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navigation_Acts#cite_note-11) passed under King Richard II provided "that, to increase the navy of England, no goods or merchandises shall be either exported or imported, but only in ships belonging to the King's subjects." The letters patent granted to the Cabots by Henry VII in 1498 stipulated that the commerce resulting from their discoveries must be with England (specifically Bristol).[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navigation_Acts#cite_note-12) Henry VIII established a second principle by statute: that such a vessel must be English-built and a majority of the crew must be English-born. Legislation during the reign of Elizabeth I also dealt with these questions and resulted in a large increase in English merchant shipping.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navigation_Acts#cite_note-ColSelf1-13) Soon after actual settlements had been made in America, these early requirements illustrate the English theory then held regarding the governmental control of maritime commerce.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navigation_Acts#cite_note-ComPolE-14)
With the establishment of overseas colonies a distinct colonial policy began to develop, and the principles embodied in the early Navigation and Trade Acts also had some more immediate precedents in the provisions of the charters granted to the London and Plymouth Company, in the various royal patents later bestowed by Charles I and Charles II, as well as in the early regulations concerning the tobacco trade, the first profitable colonial export. An Order in Council of 24 October 1621 prohibited the Colony of Virginia to export tobacco and other commodities to foreign countries.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navigation_Acts#cite_note-AndrCofT&P-15)

## Tallinn, Estonia: A Well-Preserved City of the Hanseatic League
Tallinn, Estonia, exceptionally well-preserved as a complete medieval city, served as a significant Hanseatic League outpost controlling trade with Russia after Novgorod’s accessibility declined. The entire old town is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, with intact city walls, towers, and a street pattern little changed since the Hanseatic era.
The Great Guild Hall, built in the 1410s, housed Tallinn’s most important merchant association and now contains part of the Estonian History Museum with exhibits on Hanseatic trade. Address: Pikk 17, 10133 Tallinn, Estonia. Website: www.ajaloomuuseum.ee.
St. Olaf’s Church, whose spire once made it one of the tallest buildings in the world, symbolized Tallinn’s (then known as Reval) wealth and importance to the Hanseatic League. Address: Lai 50, 10133 Tallinn, Estonia. Website: www.oleviste.ee.
The medieval Town Hall Square, surrounded by merchant houses with stepped gables, presents an ensemble of Hanseatic architecture little changed in its essential character. Address: Raekoja plats 1, 10146 Tallinn, Estonia.

## Visby, Sweden: A UNESCO City of the Hanseatic League
Visby, located on the Swedish island of Gotland in the Baltic Sea, was an early leader in Baltic trade before being eclipsed by mainland cities and suffering conquest by Denmark in 1361. The city’s medieval walls survive almost completely intact, encircling a town center where ruined churches and preserved merchant houses testify to Visby’s Hanseatic past.
The Gotland Museum presents exhibits on the island’s medieval prosperity and its role in the Hanseatic League, including hoards of coins that reveal the extent of Visby’s trading connections. Address: Strandgatan 14, 621 56. Website: www.gotlandsmuseum.se.
The entire medieval town of Visby is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and walking its streets provides a sense of a Hanseatic city frozen at an earlier moment in the confederation’s development, before the later elaboration seen in cities that remained prosperous longer.
These cities represent only the most accessible and well-preserved examples of Hanseatic heritage available to travelers in 2026. Many other former members of the Hanseatic League—Riga, Rostock, Stralsund, Wismar, Kampen, Deventer—also preserve significant medieval architecture and maintain museums exploring their Hanseatic past. For cruise passengers with limited time in port, prioritizing the old town centers of these cities and seeking out the characteristic elements of Hanseatic architecture—brick Gothic churches, stepped-gable merchant houses, medieval warehouses, and harbor installations—will provide the most rewarding encounters with this remarkable historical confederation. The legacy of the Hanseatic League offers a lens through which to understand northern Europe’s medieval development and to appreciate how commercial enterprise and urban culture created a prosperous, interconnected world centuries before our modern age of globalization.
